deep.reconstruction:
The page is a fair-copy table, page 22 of a continuous series (pp. 21–23 cover A = 0.960 … 1.200). It is a table of Gaussian addition/subtraction logarithms.

Columns, in modern notation:
- Column 1, argument A, in steps of 0.001 (left half 1.040–1.080, right half 1.080–1.120).
- Column 2, B(A) = log10(1 + 10^(-A)) = log10(1 + 1/a), where A = log10 a, given to 5 decimals.
- Column 3, the first difference of B in units of 10^-5, written between consecutive rows.
- Column 4, C(A) = A + B(A) = log10(1 + 10^A) = log10(1 + a).
- Column 5, the first difference of C in units of 10^-5.

Identification of the function (my verification):
- At A = 1 (previous page) B = 0.04139 = log10(1.1).
- At A = 1.04, 10^(-1.04) = 0.0912011 and log10(1.0912011) = 0.037904, giving 0.03790.
- At A = 1.12, 10^(-1.12) = 0.0758578 and log10(1.0758578) = 0.0317549, giving 0.03175.
- At A = 1.2 (next page) B = 0.02657.

Internal structure:
- Because C = A + B and A advances by 0.001 = 100 units, ΔB + ΔC = 100 in every row. The pairs (8,92), (9,91), (7,93) on this page bear this out.
- C is formed by simple addition of A and B.
- ΔB decreases slowly from about 8–9 to about 7 across the page, since dB/dA = -1/(1 + 10^A).

Purpose: the table lets one find log(a+b) from log a and log b without returning to numbers. Set A = log(b/a). Then log(a+b) = log a + C(A) = log b + B(A).

This is the working copy of the table Gauss published in 1812 in Zach's Monatliche Correspondenz. That table uses the same A, B, C layout and the same 5-place, 0.001-step style in this range.
errors: No computational errors found. Recomputation at A = 1.040, 1.060, 1.080, 1.093, 1.110 and 1.120 matches all entries to 5 places, every C = A + B, and every difference pair sums to 100.

The image shows corrected or overwritten digits that are now correct: the 7 in C(1.093) = 1.12671, the final 7 in B(1.110) = 0.03247 and C(1.110) = 1.14247, and some overwritten 92/93 differences around A = 1.087–1.089.

results.what: Table of B(A) = log10(1+10^-A) and C(A) = A + B(A) = log10(1+10^A) for A = 1.040 to 1.120, step 0.001, 5 decimals, with first differences
results.modern_name: Gaussian logarithms (addition/subtraction logarithms, Zech logarithms in the real case)
results.usually_credited_to: Idea due to Z. Leonelli (1802/1803). The standard table was published by Gauss in 1812 (Monatliche Correspondenz), hence the name 'Gaussian logarithms'.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript page of Gauss's own well-known table of addition logarithms (published 1812, eponymous). It is routine tabulation and offers no new mathematics, only documentary value for how the published table was prepared.
